description: We are Water Detectives from Hosur, India. I am a 12-year-old student who builds electronics and Python projects. I have made a CanSat-style satellite with a Raspberry Pi Pico and sensors, and I am building a hand-held water tester with an ESP32 that checks TDS, pH, turbidity and temperature. For Space Apps I want to use NASA Earth data to spot water and climate trends. Skills: Python, ESP32, sensors, 3D design in Tinkercad. This is a family team and we are not looking for new members.
summary: Trend Detective is a free web app that turns anyone into an Earth data detective. You click any place on a world map or type a city name. The app downloads 45 years of monthly NASA POWER data (MERRA-2 model plus satellites) for 8 variables, including temperature, rainfall, soil wetness and sunlight. It draws the time series, fits a trend line, and tests it with two statistical tests (t-test and Mann-Kendall). Then it says in plain words what is changing, where, by how much, and whether the change is significant. It can also remove the seasonal cycle, compare seasons, compare two places, build a trend map of the area around the place, project the trend to 2050, and download a report and the raw data.
details:
WHY WE BUILT IT

We built it because our borewell water was not so good, and I wanted to know how the soil is in Hosur: whether it is soft and moist, or dry. In Hosur, the main job is harvesting. So I made this app to help increase the harvest and food production. I used NASA data to find out what Hosur is like, how well farming can be done there, and how much water we need. After making it, I was very surprised because the output was really nice.

WHAT IT DOES

Trend Detective answers the four questions the challenge asks: what is changing, where, how much, and is it significant.

1. Choose a place. Click the map, type any city or village, or pick a demo place: Hosur, my school in Hosur, Arctic, Sahara, Amazon, Chennai, Antarctica.

2. Choose a variable. 8 NASA POWER variables, each with a plain-language definition: air temperature, max and min temperature, rainfall, root-zone soil wetness, humidity, wind speed, and sunlight at the ground.

3. See the trend. A graph shows every month, the trend line, and a dotted line projected into the future (up to 2100).

4. Get the verdict. Rising or falling, change per decade, total change, and a verdict: SIGNIFICANT (both tests p < 0.05), MAYBE (one test), or NOT SIGNIFICANT, explained in simple words.

ADVANCED TABS

- All variables: every variable at once in a table, with trends as a percent of the average so they can be compared.

- By season: winter, summer, monsoon and post-monsoon trends separately.

- Trend map: the same analysis at 9 points around the place, drawn as circles. Size shows strength, colour shows direction, and solid circles are significant. This shows the challenge's warning that neighbouring regions can trend in different directions.

- Compare: two places side by side.

- Report & data: a downloadable report and the raw NASA data as CSV, so anyone can check the result.

HOW IT WORKS

One call to the NASA POWER API brings monthly values for all variables from 1981. The app can remove the seasonal cycle by subtracting each calendar month's long-term average. It fits a least-squares trend with a 95% confidence interval and t-test, a Theil-Sen robust slope, and a Mann-Kendall trend test.

TOOLS

Python, Streamlit, folium + OpenStreetMap (maps), SciPy (statistics), Matplotlib (graphs), requests (NASA API). Hosted free on Streamlit Community Cloud.

EXAMPLE FINDINGS (1990-2025)

- Hosur, India, air temperature (yearly averages): rising +0.13 °C per decade, about +0.44 °C in total. Not significant yet (Mann-Kendall p = 0.079). With the season removed month by month the p-values get smaller, but monthly values are not independent, so we trust the yearly result more. The method matters.

- Tokyo, Japan, air temperature (season removed): rising +0.27 °C per decade, about +0.95 °C in total. Significant (both p < 0.001). Every point on the trend map around Tokyo is warming.

WHO IT IS FOR

Students and the public. Every variable has a simple definition, and demo places let new users try it in one click.

NEXT STEPS

Add GPM rainfall and GLDAS streamflow from NASA Earthdata. Link it to the Water Detective, an ESP32 water tester we are building, so the device shows the NASA trend for its location next to live water readings.
